thread.title: Hot Springs Board of Directors approves more than $2.5 million in midyear budget adjustments
thread.title_full: Hot Springs Board of Directors approves more than $2.5 million in midyear budget adjustments

author: @TheSenRec
title: Hot Springs Board of Directors approves more than $2.5 million in midyear budget adjustments
text:
More than $2.5 million in midyear budget adjustments the Hot Springs Board of Directors approved earlier this month included $2.3 million for the ladder truck the fire department bought for its new station at First Security Way.
City Manager Bill Burrough went over the changes at the board's 2027 goal setting work session Aug. 25. They were part of the consent agenda the board adopted at its Sept. 15 business meeting. The annual request to adjust under appropriated line items typically comes to the board in the third quarter.
Amendment 78 financing has been how large capital purchases like fire apparatuses and heavy equipment have been funded in previous years, but the city elected to pay for the fire truck outright with the large general fund balance it's been building the last five years. Local governments can finance purchases with a useful life of one year or longer for up to five years under Amendment 78 of the state Constitution.
Assistant Fire Chief Casey Burch said the 2026 Pierce Enforcer went into service last month. It replaced the 2001 Ferrara aerial apparatus that was housed at the new station.
"The new aerial features a 100-foot ladder and a special rear steer capability, which allows for maximum mobility when traveling on narrow streets and making sharp turns," Burch said. "It is equipped with a waterway and nozzles capable of flowing 2,000 gallons per minute when supplied with water from an engine."
Including the $2.3 million for the fire truck, the general fund is projected to end the year with more than $36 million in unrestricted funds, according to information the finance department provided. The projection included $519,967 left from the city's $11.7 million American Rescue Plan Act allocation the board unrestricted earlier this month.
Using fund balance to buy the fire truck is projected to create a budget deficit at year's end, with $41.4 million in expenses exceeding projected revenue by $1.4 million.
Budget adjustments approved earlier this month included $77,000 the board added to fuel line items in the solid waste fund budget. District 5 Director Karen Garcia asked Burrough last month if the increases were related to the war with Iran.
"When we developed the 2026 budget, we didn't know we were going to bomb Iran," Burrough replied. "Fuel prices have escalated. This is a direct result of that."
Another $100,000 was added to the solid waste fund in preparation for the $6 per ton increase in tipping fees the city will begin paying to landfill its Class 1 waste at the Republic Services Saline County Landfill next month. The city and other members of the Southwest Central Regional Solid Waste Management District agreed to a $25.25 per ton fee.
District members pay $19.25 under the seven-year agreement that expires at the end of the month. The district said Republic Services submitted the only responsive bid to its solicitation for waste disposal.
The city and Garland County take their Class 1 waste, or degradable garbage, to Saline County. The Garland County Landfill is only permitted for Class 4 waste, or construction demolition and debris and bulky items like furniture and appliances. Burrough said the city takes about 40,000 tons a year of Class 1 waste to Saline County.
The airport fund budget was increased to pay for a $30,000 midyear premium increase for liability insurance related to several large claims and $45,000 to repair storm damage to a hangar and aircraft. Burrough said a significant claim resulted from damage the city did to a jet hangared at the airport.
"The wing hit the tractor as they were towing it out," he told the board. "As he disconnected the plane it rolled forward and jumped its chalk. It was a significant amount of money to fix it."
